essays.essayTitle: Monopoly Power: Benefits to Consumers

sections.summary: Economies of scale may lower prices
sections.point: A high market share can benefit consumers through lower prices.
logic: Large sales and output increase the scale of input purchases
Suppliers may offer bulk-buying discounts
Lower input costs per unit reduce LRAC from C1 to C2
The firm can lower its price while maintaining a viable profit margin
If cost savings are passed on, consumers pay less and consumer surplus rises

sections.summary: Cost savings may raise profits instead
sections.point: However, a high market share may reduce the incentive to pass cost savings on to consumers.
logic: Greater market power reduces competitive pressure to cut prices
The firm may keep its price unchanged despite lower LRAC
Cost savings increase the profit margin instead
The gain in consumer welfare is limited

sections.point: The significance of the benefit depends on how much of the cost saving is passed on to consumers.
logic: A high proportion passed on through lower prices produces a larger gain in consumer surplus
A high proportion retained as profit leaves consumers with little benefit
The pass-through of savings therefore matters more than the cost reduction alone

sections.point: A high market share may benefit consumers through greater investment in product development.
logic: Strong brand loyalty and fewer close substitutes may make demand relatively price inelastic
Greater market power permits higher prices and supernormal profit
Retained profits provide funds for R&D
Successful R&D improves product quality and meets consumer needs more closely
Consumer utility increases

sections.point: However, unsuccessful R&D may raise costs without improving products.
logic: Substantial development spending may fail to produce a successful product
Costs rise without a genuine improvement in quality
If these costs are passed on, consumers face higher prices
Consumers pay more without receiving greater utility

sections.point: Consumer benefit depends more on the nature and success of innovation than on the amount spent on R&D.
logic: Innovation that meets consumer needs increases utility
High spending without meaningful product improvement offers little benefit
Sustained consumer gains therefore require successful innovation, not simply large R&D budgets

Greater price-making ability allows higher future prices
A higher price may increase the profit margin
Revenue maximisation may therefore be a strategy rather than the ultimate objective

sections.summary: Depends on the firm's market position
sections.point: The more realistic objective depends on the firm’s position in the market.
logic: While reducing LRAC and expanding market share, revenue maximisation may be more realistic

sections.point: The divorce of ownership from control may make revenue maximisation more realistic for large firms.

Managers prefer a higher output target
Output expands beyond the profit-maximising point where MR = MC

Shareholder dissatisfaction increases

They may give greater priority to profit to satisfy shareholders

sections.point: Interdependence in an oligopoly may trigger a price war that reduces firms’ profits.
logic: Each firm considers how rivals will respond to a price change
If B maintains its price, A can raise its payoff from 10 to 15 by cutting
Once A cuts, B can improve its payoff from 5 to 7 by also cutting
The same incentive applies to A, so both firms cut prices
Both receive 7 rather than the 10 each would receive by maintaining prices
Individually rational decisions leave both firms worse off

sections.point: However, firms may end a price war when sustained price cuts offer little advantage.

Profit margins remain lower

Prices may rise again, making the price war temporary

sections.summary: Depends on how long prices remain low
sections.point: The significance of a price war depends on whether low prices persist in the long run.
logic: Repeated price cuts keep margins low and make the disadvantage significant
If firms stop price competition and tacitly coordinate, prices may recover quickly
The duration of low prices determines the sustained loss of profit

sections.point: Non-price competition can impose high costs on firms in an oligopoly.

Fewer close substitutes make demand less price elastic
The firm can charge a higher price without losing many customers
If extra revenue exceeds extra cost, profit increases

sections.summary: Compare additional revenue with additional costs

sections.summary: Rising variable costs may force shutdown

AVC may rise above the average revenue received
Total revenue no longer covers variable costs
Continuing production would add to losses relative to shutting down
The firm ceases production

sections.point: However, government support that reduces variable costs may allow a firm to continue operating.

AVC may fall below AR
Revenue once again covers variable costs and contributes towards fixed costs
The firm can continue producing

essays.essayTitle: Non-price Competition: Benefits to Consumers and Businesses
essays.question: Discuss the benefits of non-price competition for consumers and businesses.

sections.point: Non-price competition can benefit consumers through higher-quality products.
logic: Firms invest more in R&D
R&D can lead to innovation and product differentiation
Product features and quality improve
Products better meet consumers' needs and preferences
Consumers gain greater choice and utility
Consumer welfare increases

sections.point: However, these benefits depend on whether R&D leads to successful innovation.
logic: Large firms may already have significant market power
Weaker competitive pressure can reduce the incentive to reinvest profits in R&D
Even when firms invest, R&D is risky and may fail
Costs may rise without genuine product improvements
Consumer utility may not increase significantly
The benefit to consumers may therefore be limited

sections.point: Advertising and branding may increase sales and profits for businesses.
logic: Advertising increases consumer awareness and familiarity
Brand loyalty becomes stronger
Consumers become less willing to switch to rivals
Demand becomes more price-inelastic
The firm can charge a higher price without losing many customers
Revenue and profit can increase
The firm may gain or protect market share

sections.point: However, non-price competition may reduce profits if its additional costs are too high.
logic: Advertising and other non-price strategies increase firms' costs
Rivals may respond with more advertising, creating an advertising race
The increase in costs may exceed the additional revenue generated
Profit margins may fall
The benefit may also be temporary if consumers switch to better rival products
Profits rise significantly only when additional revenue and long-term brand loyalty outweigh the additional cost

essays.essayTitle: Shutdown Decision: Normal Profit and Costs
essays.question: Evaluate the view that a business will always shut down if it is not able to make a normal profit.

sections.point: If a firm cannot cover its total costs in the long run, it is likely to shut down.
logic: Failure to make normal profit means AR is below AC
Total revenue is below total cost, so the firm makes a loss
Persistent losses reduce financial reserves
The firm becomes less able to pay workers, suppliers and other costs
In the long run, all costs are variable
The firm must cover total costs including opportunity cost to remain in the market
Persistent AR below AC makes continued operation unsustainable
Shutdown becomes increasingly likely

sections.point: However, failing to make normal profit does not necessarily mean the firm should shut down immediately.
logic: The loss may only be temporary
A temporary fall in demand can push AR below AC
Demand may later recover
AR may rise and the firm may return to normal profit
Shutdown can also create exit costs and make later re-entry difficult
The firm may therefore remain open if managers expect conditions to recover

sections.summary: Duration of losses and financial position
sections.point: The shutdown decision depends on whether the loss is temporary or persistent and whether the firm has enough finance to survive it.
logic: Strong cash reserves or access to credit allow the firm to tolerate losses for longer
This gives the firm time to wait for demand to recover
Weak liquidity may force the firm to close even if future conditions are expected to improve
The duration of the loss and the firm's financial position therefore affect the shutdown decision

sections.summary: AR above AVC supports continued production
sections.point: In the short run, a firm may continue operating even if it cannot make normal profit.
logic: AR can be below AC while remaining above AVC
The firm makes a loss but revenue still covers all variable costs
Revenue also makes a contribution towards fixed costs
If the firm shuts down, revenue falls to zero while fixed costs remain
The firm would lose its contribution towards fixed costs
Continuing production therefore minimises the firm's loss
The firm should remain open in the short run while AR is above AVC

/diagrams/shutdown-normal-profit-kaa2.jp.alt: Short-run shutdown diagram showing MC, AC and AVC with P1 and P2.
/diagrams/shutdown-normal-profit-kaa2.jp.caption: Short-run shutdown decision: a loss-making firm can continue while AR remains above AVC.

sections.point: However, if AR falls below AVC, shutting down is the loss-minimising decision.
logic: Revenue is not enough to cover the variable costs of production
Continued production adds more to variable cost than it generates in revenue
Each additional unit therefore increases the firm's total loss
Shutdown allows the firm to avoid variable costs
Fixed costs still remain in the short run
Once AR falls below AVC, shutdown minimises losses

sections.point: The short-run shutdown rule is important, but the firm's objectives, expectations and financial position can affect how long it continues operating.
logic: A firm may prioritise survival or long-term growth over short-run profit
It may accept losses while establishing a customer base or waiting for demand to recover
This strategy is sustainable only if the firm has enough finance to fund the losses
The final shutdown decision therefore depends on both the cost condition and the firm's ability and willingness to continue

essays.essayTitle: State-owned vs Private-sector Business Objectives
essays.question: Evaluate the view that the objectives of state-owned enterprises and private sector organisations always differ.

source.filename: State-owned vs private-sector business objectives --2023.1 Q8.docx

sections.summary: Private firms may prioritise profit maximisation
sections.point: Private-sector organisations may prioritise profit maximisation because shareholders expect financial returns.
logic: Shareholders invest capital and may expect dividends or capital growth
Managers face pressure to generate profit
Profit maximisation occurs where MC = MR
Private firms can charge for services to cover costs and earn profit
The profit objective may therefore be stronger than for a fully subsidised state enterprise

/diagrams/state-owned-private-objectives.alt: Diagram comparing profit maximisation at Q1 and P1 with allocative efficiency at Q2 and P2.
/diagrams/state-owned-private-objectives.caption: Private-sector profit maximisation can be compared with a state-owned enterprise pursuing allocative efficiency.
/diagrams/state-owned-private-objectives.sourceLocation: State-owned vs private-sector business objectives --2023.1 Q8.docx · word/media/image2.jpeg

sections.summary: Private firms may also pursue social objectives
sections.point: However, private ownership does not mean that an organisation only pursues profit.
logic: Consumers may value socially responsible behaviour
The private firm may adopt social or environmental objectives to protect its reputation and demand
Stronger demand can increase revenue
Social objectives may therefore support long-run profit
Private-sector and state-owned objectives may overlap

sections.summary: Depends on shareholder and stakeholder pressure
sections.point: The difference between private and state-owned objectives depends on shareholder and stakeholder pressure.
logic: Strong shareholder pressure for financial returns makes profit maximisation more likely
Objectives differ more from those of a socially focused state enterprise
Consumers who value social outcomes reward similar private behaviour
The objectives become more similar

sections.summary: State firms may prioritise social welfare
sections.point: State-owned enterprises may prioritise social welfare and allocative efficiency rather than profit maximisation.
logic: The government owns the organisation and can direct it to provide services
Allocative efficiency occurs where P = MC
Output increases from Q1 to Q2
Price falls from P1 to P2
Lower price and higher output increase access to the service
Social welfare and social mobility improve

sections.summary: State firms may pursue commercial objectives
sections.point: However, state ownership does not rule out commercial objectives.
logic: Persistent losses require larger government subsidies
Subsidies create an opportunity cost because funds could be used elsewhere
The government may require the enterprise to cover its costs or earn a profit
Some state-owned enterprises may generate revenue for the government
Their objectives become more similar to those of private-sector organisations

sections.summary: Depends on the government's budget constraint
sections.point: The difference depends on the strength of the government's budget constraint.
logic: Sufficient public funding allows greater priority to access and social welfare
Objectives differ more from those of a profit-maximising private organisation
Limited funding makes financial sustainability more important
The objectives are more likely to converge with those of private organisations
